The buzzing had gone down to a hum, far away, like a fridge in another room. My body was a long, heavy, aching thing lying on a wet sheet. My mouth tasted of metal and bitterness and sick.
I opened my eyes.
The window was grey. The sea was grey. Dawn. The fan was still turning.
The doctor was asleep in the leather armchair in the corner, sitting up, with her head on one side and her glasses in her lap.
Chela was standing at the window with her back to me, looking out at the sea, with her arms folded across her grey cardigan.

I knew who she was. I am telling you that plainly, because it would be dishonest to pretend I did not. I knew in the way you know something at the end of a long illness, when you are too tired to argue with it any more. Her face had not been the medicine. It had been her face.
I did not say anything. I could not have said anything. My tongue was a dead thing in my mouth.
I lay and watched her back for a long time, as the room got lighter.
I had come to this house because someone had told me that the medicine would take everything I had done wrong off me, like a coat. That I would come back new.
It had not taken anything off me. It had put everything on.
ANOTHER NIGHT
The morning after

A writer named Kevin Franciotti went to a clinic called La Misión [lah mee-SYOHN], in Baja California [BAH-hah kah-lee-FOR-nyah], not far from the white house. He had his own reasons for going, and he wanted to know what the root would do to him. He wrote about it afterwards, plainly, without making it sound better than it was.

The night, he said, was loud. A buzzing that filled his head. A feeling of being pulled down a tunnel. Then hours of pictures, flashing and bursting, like a fireworks show that would not end. It was strange and long and hard, and he got through it.
It was the next day that frightened him.

The fireworks had stopped. The visions had gone. He was lying in a bed in a quiet room in daylight, and he was still in it. His body was heavy. He could not sleep. He could not get up. His mind, which should have been empty and tired, was not empty. It was turning over everything he had ever done wrong. Every person he had let down. Every lie. Not as pictures now. As plain thoughts, one after another, in full daylight, with nothing to hide behind.
He felt guilt like a weight on his chest. He felt panic. He felt that it would not end.

This is the part the websites leave out. The night is the part people tell stories about, because the night is strange and the stories are good. But the drug does not stop when the night stops. What the body makes from it stays in the blood for a day and more, sometimes for several. The pictures go, but the thinking stays on, and it is slow, and it is grey, and you are wide awake for all of it.
The people who work in these clinics have a name for it. They call it the grey day.
Some of them say the grey day is where the real work is done. That the night shows you, but the day makes you hold it.
Kevin Franciotti held it. He got up, in the end. He went home. He kept writing.
In the white house, the curtains were half open, and it was morning, and the doctor was asleep in Chela’s chair.
IV. THE GREY DAY
Everybody who has been through this medicine talks about the day after. They call it the grey day. I had read the phrase somewhere and thought it sounded gentle, like a cloudy Sunday.
It is not gentle. I will tell you what it is, plainly.

The medicine itself does not last all that long in the body. A few hours. But the liver turns it into a second substance, a close cousin of the first, and the second one lasts much longer. A day. Two days. Sometimes more. It is quieter than the first. It does not show you films. What it does is keep you awake, and keep everything turned up.

So on the grey day you cannot sleep. You lie there with your eyes open, completely exhausted, more tired than you have ever been in your life, and sleep will not come, not for a minute. Every sound is too loud. A door closing at the other end of the house is a gunshot. Somebody’s spoon against a cup in the kitchen goes through your head like a nail. The light is too bright. Your balance is still gone, so if you sit up, the room slides. You cannot eat. Your body aches everywhere, as if you have been beaten, and in a way you have.

And your mind is very, very clear. Not happy. Not sad. Clear, like water in a glass. Everything you saw in the night is still there, sitting in front of you, and you cannot stop looking at it, and you cannot pretend you did not see it, because the medicine is still in you, holding your face in both hands.
That is the grey day.

The doctor woke up in the armchair, stiff, and looked at the monitor before she looked at me. Fifty-eight beats a minute. The resetting time was still long, but shorter than in the night. She took the strip of paper that had been printing all night from the machine, and stood by the window with it, pulling it through her fingers, metre by metre, reading it the way you read a long letter.
When she got to the place at 2:40 she stopped for a long time.
Then she folded the strip up into a thick square, and held it in her hand, and came and sat on the edge of the bed.
She looked tired. She looked about ten years older than she had the day before.
“Where are they?” she said.
I did not pretend. I did not have it in me. The medicine was still holding my face.
“In my bag,” I said. “Under the socks. At the bottom.”
She went to the bag and found them and read the label and put the bottle on the table beside the bed, very carefully, where I could see it. Then she sat down again.
“You know what those do with my medicine,” she said.
“Yes.”
“You knew when you filled in the form.”
“Yes.”
“You are a professional. You know the red list better than I do.”
“Yes.”
She was quiet for a while. Outside, the sea. Somewhere in the house, a door closed, and it went through my head like a nail.

“Three people,” she said. “Three people have died in this house in eleven years. One was a man who had a bad heart and did not know. One was a man who smoked heroin in the bathroom on the grey day, when his body had forgotten how to take it. One was a woman who lied on her form. Like you.”
I did not say anything.
“I go to their funerals,” she said. “Every one. I go and I sit at the back and I do not speak to anyone. I want you to know that. Last night I very nearly had to go to yours.”
Then she told me the name of the medicine.

I want to tell you exactly how she did it, because it was not how I expected. I expected her to tell me as a punishment, or as a doctor reading out a diagnosis. She told it the way you tell somebody a secret you think they have earned.
She said: “You came all this way and you never asked me what it is. Everybody asks. You never asked once.”
“I didn’t want to know,” I said. “I didn’t want to know what I was taking. I just wanted it to work.”
“That is the most honest thing you have said since you came here,” she said. “So now I will tell you. It is called ibogaine [ih-BOH-gah-een]. It comes from a plant called iboga [ih-BOH-gah].”
I said it back to her. Ibogaine. It sounded like a name from a fairy tale. Like the name of a witch, or a country under a mountain.
“Now,” the doctor said, “you cannot sleep anyway. So I will tell you what you have in your blood. All of it. The good and the bad. And you will lie there and listen, because you cannot go anywhere.”
And she did. She sat on the edge of the bed for an hour, in the grey light, with her reading glasses on and the folded strip of my heartbeat in her pocket, and told me everything.
I will tell it to you the way she told it to me.

Iboga is a shrub. A bush, about as tall as a man, with shiny green leaves and small white and pink flowers, and little orange fruits like olives. It grows wild in the shade of the rainforest of west-central Africa, mostly in a country called Gabon, on the Atlantic coast, right on the equator, and in the countries around it.

The part that matters is the root. If you dig the bush up and scrape the bark off the root, the scrapings are yellowish and bitter, very bitter, so bitter they make your mouth go numb. That bitterness is the medicine. In the bark of the root there are a dozen different natural substances, and the strongest of them is ibogaine.
The people in Gabon have known about it for a very long time. Nobody knows how long. Hundreds of years, at least.
Hunters used to chew a little of the root to stay awake on long hunts, and to go without food and water. A little iboga is like a very strong cup of coffee.
But a lot of iboga is something else.

In Gabon there is a religion called Bwiti [BWEE-tee]. It is very old, and it has changed many times, and in the last hundred years it has mixed with Christianity, so that today some Bwiti churches have crosses in them as well as drums. Iboga is at the centre of it.

When a young person is initiated into Bwiti, they eat a great deal of the root bark, much more than any hunter would, over a long night, and sometimes several, in a temple, with music and singing and torches, and with older members of the church sitting around them to watch over them. Then they lie down, and they go a very long way.

The people of Bwiti have a phrase for what happens. It is sometimes translated into English as breaking open the head, or cracking the skull. The idea is that the root opens your head like a door, and you go out through it, and travel.

They say you travel to the land of the dead. That you meet your ancestors there, the people of your family who died before you, and they talk to you, and teach you, and show you things about your own life. Then you come back. And the people who come back are said to be new, like children just born, with the old things washed off them.

“That is what is on our website,” the doctor said. “Like a child that has just been born. I did not write that. The man who owns this house wrote it. He likes it because it sells. It is not wrong, exactly. But he leaves out the most important part.”
“What’s the most important part?”

“The Bwiti do not say that the root takes your wrongs away,” she said. “That is how foreigners tell it. Americans. Europeans. People who want to be forgiven for something by Monday. What the Bwiti say, as I understand it, from the ones I have talked to, is that the root makes you see what you did. You have to look at all of it. Then perhaps you are new. Not before.” She took her glasses off and rubbed her eyes. “Nobody wants to pay eight thousand five hundred dollars to look. Everybody wants to pay to be washed.”
The rest of the world found the root very late.

In 1901, French chemists took the strongest substance out of the root bark and gave it a name, ibogaine. For about thirty years, from the 1930s to the 1960s, it was sold in chemists’ shops in France as a tonic, in little tablets, to help tired people and sick people feel stronger. Nobody in France thought of it as a door to anywhere. It was a pick-me-up, like a vitamin.
Then, in 1962, it fell into the hands of a nineteen-year-old in New York City.

His name was Howard Lotsof [LOT-sof]. He was a heroin addict. He was looking, he said later, for a new way to get high, and someone gave him a bitter white powder made from the iboga root, and he took it. He was in it for more than a day. And when he came out of it, he noticed something that nobody had ever noticed before, because nobody who was addicted to heroin had ever taken it.
He did not want heroin any more.

Not a little less. Not at all. The sickness of withdrawal, the shaking and the sweating and the aching that every heroin addict knows and dreads, was not there. And the wanting was not there. He said, years afterwards, that during the night he had come to see heroin as something that copied death, and that he had decided he would rather live.
He gave it to some friends who were also using heroin. Six of them, he said. Five of them stopped.

Howard Lotsof spent the rest of his life trying to make the world take that seriously. It was very hard. In the United States, a few years after his discovery, ibogaine was put on the list of the most strictly forbidden drugs, with heroin and LSD, as something with no medical use at all. It is still on that list today. It is illegal to have it anywhere in my country.
“So how do you have it?” I said. “Here?”

“Here, nobody says it is legal and nobody says it is illegal,” the doctor said. “Mexico does not have a law about it. So we use it. That is why the clinics are all here, along the coast, half an hour from your border. Americans come down, and go back up.”
“And it works? For addiction?”
She thought about it, honestly, the way I think about a patient’s numbers before I say anything to the family.

“For some people, it is a miracle,” she said. “I have seen it. People who used heroin for twenty years walk out of this house and never touch it again. I have letters on my wall from them. For some people, it does nothing. They are back on the street in Tijuana by the weekend. For most people, it is something in the middle. It takes away the sickness of stopping, and it takes away the wanting, for a few weeks, or a few months. A window. A door that opens for a while. What they do with that door is up to them.”
“How does it work?”

“Nobody knows,” she said. “Truly. I tell everybody this. It is not like most medicines, that fit one lock in the brain, like a key. Ibogaine touches a dozen locks at once, all over the brain, a little of this, a little of that. Somewhere in all that touching, it seems to reset something. Like turning a computer off and on again. But which lock does it, nobody knows yet. They are still arguing.”
“And it kills people,” I said.
“Yes,” the doctor said. “It kills people. You know how. Last night you almost found out from the inside.”

She told me the numbers, the real ones, the way they are written in the medical journals. In 2012, a group of doctors went through every death they could find anywhere outside Africa where somebody had died after taking ibogaine. Between 1990 and 2008 they found nineteen. Later reviews have found more. Most of the people had hearts that were already weak, or had other drugs in their bodies at the same time, or were treated in someone’s apartment or a motel room by people with no training and no monitor. One estimate is that something like one in every three hundred people who take it dies.
“One in three hundred,” I said. “In my hospital we would never—”

“No,” she said. “In your hospital you would never. In your hospital you have rules and lawyers and a defibrillator on every wall. And in your hospital you do not have ibogaine. So the people who want it come here, to me, and to houses much worse than this one, and some of them lie on the form.”
I looked at the pill bottle on the table.

“The heart is the danger,” she said. “Always the heart. You saw why. It makes the reset slower. If the reset is already slow, from another medicine, or a weak heart, or low salts in the blood, then you are standing on the edge of a cliff, and the medicine is a strong wind.”
The last thing she told me surprised me.
“It is changing,” she said. “Slowly. Your country is starting to look.”

In January 2024, a team of doctors from Stanford University, one of the best universities in America, published a study in a very serious medical journal. They had followed thirty American soldiers from the special forces. Hard men. Men who had been blown up, many times, in many wars, and had come home with their brains damaged and their minds full of what they had seen, and could not sleep, and could not stop drinking, and some of them wanted to die.
The soldiers came to a clinic in Mexico, like this one, a few miles down this same coast. They were given ibogaine. And they were given magnesium with it, through a drip, to protect the heart.
“Magnesium,” I said.
“Yes,” she said, and gave me a long look. “The same thing I put into your vein at 2:50 this morning.”

One month afterwards, the soldiers’ worst symptoms had dropped by more than eighty per cent. Their nightmares, their depression, their fear. Their memories and concentration got better. Nobody’s heart stopped. The doctors who wrote it up said they had never seen anything like it.

And in June 2025, the state of Texas decided to spend fifty million dollars of public money to help run proper scientific trials of ibogaine, so that one day, maybe, it can be a real medicine in America, given in real hospitals, with monitors, and rules, and lawyers, and defibrillators on the wall.
“One day,” the doctor said, “you will be able to have this in Albuquerque, and nobody will have to lie to anybody to get it.” She stood up. “Not this year.”
She went to the door. Then she stopped with her hand on the handle and turned round.
“Last night,” she said. “You talked. All night. You know that?”
“Yes,” I said. “I think I know.”
“I did not hear it,” she said. “I was asleep. I want you to know that. I did not hear a word.” She looked at me for a moment longer. “I am not the one who was awake.”
She went out, and closed the door very softly, and it went through my head like a nail.
Chela came back at two in the afternoon.

She was not on duty. Her shift was the nights. She came in through the door without knocking, in different clothes, a blue dress and a straw bag over her shoulder, like a woman on her way to the market, and she pulled the leather armchair over from the corner, right up close to the bed, and sat in it.
She did not have her notebook.
The light was very bright. It hurt my eyes. I could not move my head. I lay and looked at her sideways, the way I had been looking at everything all day, like a glass of water on a tray.
“I know who you are,” I said.
“I know you know,” she said. “You’ve been looking at me since six o’clock this morning like I’m a ghost.”
“What’s your name?”

“Graciela [grah-see-EH-lah],” she said. “Graciela Ortiz [or-TEES]. Chela is short for Graciela. Everybody’s called me that since I was a baby. My son called me Mama. But when he wanted something, he called me Chela, to be funny. Ay, Chela, por favor [eye, CHEH-lah, por fah-BOR]. Oh, Chela, please.”

I had read her name in the newspaper nearly seven years before. I had read it many times. Graciela Ortiz, 44, mother of the victim, who works at the hospital laundry. I had read it and folded the paper and put it in the bin, and taken the bin out, so that it would not be in the flat.

I had never seen her face. At the sentencing I had sat at the back, in sunglasses, and looked at no one. I had never gone to the funeral. I had seen her once, from a car, out of the corner of my eye, kneeling in the dirt in a grey coat.

I want to tell you what she told me that afternoon. I will tell it plainly, in her order, the way she told it. She had clearly told it to herself many times, and it came out of her smooth and flat, worn down like a step.

After Mateo died, she went to the cross every Sunday for a year and a half. She could not stay in the house. Every room in the house was him. She could not go on folding sheets in the hospital laundry, in the basement, with the clock on the wall that said ten past eleven every night. In the summer of 2021 she gave up the house and moved to Rosarito, to live with her own mother, who was old and needed looking after, in a little concrete house two streets back from the sea.

She got a job in a laundry in Tijuana. Then her mother died. Then she got this job, sitting with patients at night, because the clinic needed someone who could stay awake, and she found she could not sleep anyway.
“Why this?” I said. “Of all the jobs.”

“Because people come here who are dying,” she said. “Slowly. Of drugs. And some of them, in one night, stop dying. I sit in the chair and I watch them come back. Every night I watch somebody come back.” She looked out of the window at the sea. “I wanted to watch it happen to somebody. Since I could not watch it happen to him.”

In the spring of 2024 a man came to the clinic for nightmares. A thin man in his thirties with very short hair, who had been in prison and could not sleep since he came out. A mechanic, from New Mexico.
She sat with him, the way she sat with me. He talked in the night, the way I talked. They all talk.

He said Dana. He said it many times. He said the keys, and she wanted the Christmas station, and I let her, I let her. And then he said the name of the road in the North Valley, and the name of the boy.

“I had my notebook on my knee,” she said. “I was writing down what he said, like always. When he said my son’s name, I wrote it down. Then I put the pen in my mouth, so I would not make a sound. I bit it. It broke. There was ink all over my teeth.” She showed me with her hand, on her mouth. “I sat there with ink on my teeth until six in the morning, and wrote down everything he said.”
“Did you tell him?”

“On the grey day,” she said. “Like this. Here. In this chair.” She put her hand on the leather arm of it, where it was worn pale. “I told him who I was. He cried for a long time. He said he was sorry. He said he should have refused you. He said he had thought about coming to me, a thousand times, and telling me, but he had promised you, and he was a man who keeps promises, even stupid ones.”
“Did he give you my number?”

“No,” she said. “He would never. He still would not, I think. He still loves you, a little. He would never give me anything of yours.” She almost smiled. “But a man who comes out of prison does not have many friends, and he leaves his phone on the table on the terrace when he goes to the bathroom.”
“So it was you,” I said. “The message. It helped me sleep.”
“Yes.”
“I thought it was him.”
“I know. That is why I wrote it like that.” She looked at me steadily. “It was true, too. It did help him sleep. He sleeps now. He told me.”
“What did you want?” I said. “When you sent it. What did you want to happen?”
She took a long time to answer. The sea went on outside, in and out, in and out.

“I wanted you to come here,” she said. “I wanted you to lie in that bed and take the medicine and go to the road. Because I knew you would. Everybody goes back to the worst place. I wanted you to have to see it. Him. Not in the newspaper. Him. The way I see him.”
“And then?”

“And then I didn’t know,” she said. “I didn’t know what I would do. I have thought about it for two years, and I didn’t know. I thought maybe I would hit you. Maybe I would spit on you. Maybe I would put a pillow on your face while you were lying there with your head like a glass of water and could not move.” She said it all quite calmly, in the same flat, worn-down voice. “I thought about all of those. Many nights. In that chair, with other people’s children in the bed.”
“And then the alarm went,” I said.
“And then the alarm went.”
“You waited.”
“Yes.”
“You counted.”

“Yes. Nine minutes. I looked at the clock on the monitor and I counted, quietly, out loud. Uno. Dos. Like you counted, on the road. You told me, at half past one, how you counted. Every six seconds, ten to a minute. Nine minutes. And at eight he stopped.” Her voice did not change. “So I counted the same. To see.”
“To see what?”
She leaned forward in the chair, close to me, so close I could smell her soap, and coffee, and the sea on her clothes. Her eyes were dark and dry and very tired.
“To see if I could,” she said. “To see if I was like you.”
We looked at each other.

“I am not,” she said. “I want you to know that. I was there at nine, with my finger on the bell. I could have gone to ten. Eleven. Twenty. Nobody would ever know. The doctor was asleep. A woman with a bad heart lies on her form, takes the medicine, dies in the night. It happens. It is in the journals. One in three hundred.” She sat back. “I rang the bell at nine. You did not ring yours at all.”
I asked her what she wanted now.

I asked it the way you ask a patient’s family, at the end, what they want done. I did not have any other way of asking it. I was lying flat on my back, unable to move my head, with my heartbeat still printing out on a strip of paper beside me. There was nothing I could give her and nothing I could stop her taking.
“I don’t want the police,” she said. “That surprises you.”
“Yes.”

“It doesn’t matter what I want. I asked a lawyer, in San Diego, last year. A woman. I paid her two hundred dollars to tell me.” She counted on her fingers, the way you count for a child. “If they found out tomorrow that you were driving, drunk, what could they charge you with? Killing my son with a car. Lying to the police. Hiding evidence. And in New Mexico, she told me, each of those crimes has a clock on it. A time limit. If they do not charge you before the clock runs out, they can never charge you. Never. Not for the rest of your life.”
“How long?” I said. I knew. I did not want to know.

“Six years for the worst one,” she said. “Five for the others. From the night it happened.” She put her hands back in her lap. “The last one ran out on the twenty-first of December last year. I sat at his cross that morning, in the cold, and watched the sun come up, and said goodbye to the law.”
I closed my eyes. Behind them it was only grey now, the ordinary grey of a tired woman’s eyelids.

“So there is nothing anybody can do to you,” she said. “Not me. Not the police. Not God, I think. I stopped believing in God the night I came home to the pot on the stove.” She stood up and pulled the strap of her straw bag onto her shoulder. “There is only what you do.”
At the door, she turned round, the way the doctor had.
“On Sunday you go home,” she said. “The van takes you to the border at noon. You walk across at the pedestrian gate. The one on the west side, by the outlet shops.”
“Yes.”

“He will be there,” she said. “Wes. On the other side. I told him what day, and what time. He did not want to come. He said he would never come. Then last night, at four in the morning, after the doctor fell asleep in the chair, I sent him a message to say you nearly died, and he wrote back: I’ll be there.”
“What does he want?”

“I don’t know,” she said. “I didn’t ask. Maybe nothing. Maybe to see your face once. Maybe he wants you to say it. Out loud. Once. To him, on the street, in daylight, with people walking past.” She shrugged. “That’s what I would want. But I am not him. He is a much kinder person than me. He might just want to drive you home.”
She went out.
The grey day went on, and on, the way grey days do.

I could not sleep. I lay and watched the light move across the wooden ceiling, and the fan go round, and listened to every sound in the house as if it were a gunshot: the boy from Ohio being sick down the corridor, and laughing afterwards, a strange high laugh; the doctor’s voice on the telephone in Spanish; a car on the coast road; gulls.
Towards evening I tried an experiment. I am a scientist, of a kind. I wanted to know.
I said out loud, in the empty room, to the fan, in my ordinary calm voice, the voice I use at work, the sentence I had said thousands of times.
“I was the passenger.”

That is what I meant to say. I opened my mouth to say it, and took the breath for it, and it would not come. My mouth would not make it. My tongue lay in my mouth like a dead thing. I tried three times. On the third time I was sick into the orange bucket instead, and lay back, shaking, with the bitter taste in my teeth.
I tried something else.
“I was driving,” I said.
It came out quite easily. Quietly, in the empty room. Three words. As easy as breathing out.

That is the only thing the medicine took from me, in the end. Not the nightmares. Not the guilt. Not my sins, whatever those are. It took away my ability to say the sentence I had lived inside for nearly seven years.
The doctor had told me that for the people who come here to stop heroin, it takes away the wanting. I had wanted nothing more, for nearly seven years, than to be the passenger.
I did not want it any more.
ANOTHER NIGHT
The forest

In the rainforest of west-central Africa there is a shrub that grows to about the height of a man. Its root is yellow under the bark. The people who have lived beside it longest scrape that bark into a powder and eat it.
For most of them it is a small thing. A pinch to stay awake on a long hunt, or through a night of dancing. But once in a life, for some, it is not a small thing at all.

There is a religion built around the root. It is called Bwiti [BWEE-tee], and it is still alive. It is practised today, in villages and in cities, by people with telephones and jobs. It is not a museum. It is not a story about the past. It belongs to the people who keep it, and what is written here is only what they have chosen to tell outsiders.
What they have told is this.

A person comes to the initiation because something is wrong, or because it is time. They are given the powder, spoon after spoon, far more than anyone would take to stay awake. Then they sit, or lie down, and the singing begins, and the harp begins, and it does not stop. People sit with them all night. Someone is always awake beside them.
The initiates say the root cracks the skull. They mean that the head is opened, and the person goes out through the opening.

Where they go is the land of the dead. Not a place of punishment. A place of the family. The grandmother who died before you were born is there. The father you buried is there. They walk with you. They show you things. Sometimes they show you a road. Sometimes the road is long, and there are things on it you did not want to see again.

The ceremony lasts for days, not one night. And when the root has worn off, there is one more thing to do. The new initiate tells the others what they saw. All of it, out loud, to people who are awake. That is part of it. You do not keep the night to yourself. Only after the telling are you counted as one of them.
That is when you are said to be born again. What you did wrong before has been seen, by you and by the dead, and said out loud, and it is taken away.
That is the promise. It is an old one, and it was not made to strangers.

Over the last thirty years, strangers have come anyway. They fly to Gabon [gah-BOHN], or to clinics far from Gabon, and they pay. They take the root, or what a laboratory has pulled out of it, and they lie down in rooms with air conditioning, and somebody sits with them, and somebody writes down the time.
What they are promised, mostly, is the morning. Born again. The past taken off.

They are not always told the other half. That in the forest, the night is not the whole of it. That what you saw on the road, you have to say out loud, to someone who is awake. That nothing is taken off you until you have.
V. THE LINE

I slept, in the end, on the Saturday night. Not much. Three hours, perhaps. It came all at once, at about two in the morning, like falling down a well, and there was nothing at the bottom of it at all. No road. No counting. Just black, and then the gulls, and grey light in the window.
It was the first night in nearly seven years that I did not dream about the road.

I want to be careful how I say that, because I know how it sounds. It sounds like the end of an advertisement. After just one night, Dana slept like a baby. It was not like that. I did not dream about the road because I did not need to dream about it any more. I had been there. I knew what was at the end of the counting. A dream is a door you have not opened. I had opened it.
Chela came to my room at nine on Sunday morning, before the van.
She was in the blue dress again, with the straw bag. She did not sit down. She took something out of the bag and held it out to me.

It was a notebook. A cheap school exercise book with a green cardboard cover, the kind you buy in a pharmacy for a few pesos, soft and bent at the corners from being carried. On the front, in pen, she had written the date. 9–10 octubre 2026 [ok-TOO-breh]. The ninth and tenth of October.
“These are your pages,” she said. “I tore them out of my real one and put them in this. The rest of my real one is other people’s. These are yours.”
I took it. It weighed almost nothing.
“You don’t want to keep it?” I said. “It’s—” I did not know what to call it. Evidence. A confession. The only record in the world, in anybody’s hand, of what happened on that road.
“I don’t need it,” she said. “I was there. I heard it.” She hitched the strap of her bag up on her shoulder. “You’re the one who keeps forgetting.”
Then she did something I did not expect. She put out her hand, and touched my cheek, very briefly, with the backs of her fingers. The way you touch a child’s face to see if they have a fever.
“You talked all night,” she said. “Six hours. You never once said you were sorry. Did you know that?”
I opened my mouth.
“Don’t,” she said. “Not now. Not to me. I don’t want it now. It’s too late for me to want it.” She took her hand away. “Say it to someone it’s not too late for.”
And she went.
I never saw her again.
The van left at half past eleven. The same young driver, who still did not ask me anything. I sat in the back, behind him. A passenger.

The boy from Ohio was in the van too, on the seat beside me, going home on the same day. He looked very different. He was still grey and thin and shaky, but his face had changed. It had come back, the way a face comes back after a long fever. He looked out of the window at the sea the whole way, and once he laughed, out loud, at nothing, at a dog on the side of the road chasing a plastic bag.
When we got to the border he shook my hand and said, “Good luck, ma’am.”
I said, “You too.”
He said, “I don’t want it. I don’t want it at all. Isn’t that crazy? I’ve wanted it every minute for six years and I don’t want it.” He was nearly crying. “I don’t know how long it’ll last.”
“Nobody does,” I said. “That’s what the doctor said. It’s a door. What you do with it is up to you.”

He nodded, very seriously, as if I had said something wise. Then he picked up his bag and walked away into the crowd, and I never saw him again either, and I think about him more than I expected to. I hope he is alive. I have no way of knowing.
From here I will tell it by the clock again, because the line at the border is like the night in the white house. It is a place where you wait, and cannot leave, and count the minutes.
The pedestrian crossing going north, into the United States, is very different from the one going south. Going south, they barely look at you. Going north, you wait.

The line started outside, on the Mexican side, along a concrete walkway with a metal roof over it to keep off the sun, and railings on both sides, so that you shuffled forward in single file like cattle at a market. Hundreds of people. Women with shopping bags. Men in work clothes. Students with backpacks. Families with small children asleep on their shoulders. Old people with walking sticks, coming back from the dentist with new teeth. A man selling bottles of water and churros [CHOO-rohs], fried dough sticks, out of a cooler, walking up and down beside the railing, calling out.
I stood in the line with my bag over my shoulder and the green notebook in my hand.
The sign said: wait time from this point approximately 50 minutes.
I read my pages while I waited.
I had not read them yet. I had held the notebook all morning, closed, in my lap, in the van, like something that might go off.

Now I opened it, standing in the line, in the heat, with the man with the churros calling out beside me, and I read what I had said in the night, in Chela’s small careful handwriting, line by line, with the times down the side.
I am not going to copy it out for you. You know what it says. I have told you all of it already.
But I will tell you one thing I had not known.

Halfway down the second page, at 01:58, between two things I said about the road, there is a short line in brackets. Chela’s handwriting, but smaller, pressed hard into the paper. It is not something I said. It is something she wrote for herself.
(Wes me dijo que dijo: Chela.) [wes meh DEE-hoh keh DEE-hoh CHEH-lah]

I did not understand it, in the line. My Spanish is hospital Spanish. Where does it hurt. Breathe in. Breathe out. I read it three times. I asked the woman in front of me in the line, an old lady with a shopping bag full of medicine boxes, what it meant. I showed her the line.
She read it, and looked at me, and then looked at the line again.
“It says,” she said, slowly, in English, “Wes told me that he said Chela.” She frowned at it. “Who is Chela?”
“The boy’s mother,” I said.
I stood in the line, and did not move, and the line moved without me, and the man behind me said, “Señora” [sen-YOR-ah], ma’am, politely, and I stepped forward.
I knew what it meant. I had been there. Not as myself. As Wes.

In the night, in the white house, the film had shown me Wes kneeling in the water, in the ditch, saying hey, hey, buddy, you’re okay, not knowing what else to do. And then it had shown me Wes turning round and shouting for me. And then it had taken me into my own eyes, at the driver’s door, and I had stayed there, at the driver’s door, for nine minutes.
From the door, in the dark, I had seen only the shape of him in the ditch. I had not seen what Wes did there.

Wes had. Wes had gone back. While I was wiping the steering wheel, he had gone back to the ditch and knelt in the water again and held the boy’s hand, because it was the only thing he could think of to do. And at some point, before eight, the boy had said one word.
He had called for his mother. The way he called her when he wanted something.
Chela.
The way you say please.

Wes had told her that, on his grey day, in the leather chair. It was the thing he had carried for four years in prison and never told anyone. Not his lawyer. Not me. The boy’s last word. And she had written it down in my pages, in brackets, at 01:58, small and hard, at the exact moment in my story when I was standing at the door of the truck.

The line went inside a long building with a low ceiling and strong air conditioning and fluorescent lights. There were signs everywhere, in English and Spanish. Have your documents ready. No photographs. No mobile phones.

At the far end there were booths. Glass booths, a row of them, each with an officer inside in a dark blue uniform, behind a window, with a computer and a camera. One person at a time stepped up to the window. The officer looked at their passport, and at their face, and asked them something, and they answered, and the officer either waved them on or pointed them to a door at the side.

It reminded me of something, and it took me a long time to understand what. Then I understood. It was the confessional. The little booths in the old church in Old Town that my grandmother took me to when I was small. A window, a person behind it, a question, an answer.
My turn.

The officer was a man in his forties with a shaved head and reading glasses pushed up on top of it, the way people wear them who need them for close work and nothing else. He took my passport and scanned it and looked at the screen and then at my face. I must have looked terrible. Grey, thin, with dark rings under my eyes, after three nights without real sleep.
“Purpose of your trip?” he said.
“Medical,” I said.
He nodded. He had heard it a thousand times. Half of San Diego goes to Tijuana for its teeth.
“Bringing anything back? Medicines, food, anything to declare?”
I stood at the window.
Anything to declare.

I want you to understand that I knew exactly what he meant. He meant: do you have pills in your bag, or cheese, or more than ten thousand dollars in cash. He meant nothing else. He was a tired man in a glass box asking the same question he asks four hundred times a day.
And I had a green school notebook in my hand with my crime written in it in another woman’s handwriting, and a medicine in my blood that would not let me say I was the passenger.
“Yes,” I said.
He looked up.
“Ma’am?”
“Nothing in the bag,” I said. “I’m sorry. I meant no. Nothing in the bag.”
He looked at me for a moment longer, the way the doctor had, the first afternoon. The look of someone who can see that you are not telling him everything and has no way to prove it.
Then he stamped nothing, because they do not stamp anything any more, and handed me back my passport, and said, “Welcome home,” and looked past me at the next person.
I walked out of the building into the sun on the American side.

It was very bright and hot. There was a wide concrete plaza, and palm trees, and the outlet shops across the road with their big coloured signs, and a trolley station, and taxis, and people everywhere, meeting, hugging, waving, dragging suitcases.
He was standing by a lamppost at the edge of the plaza, in the shade, with his hands in the pockets of his jeans.

He was thinner than in the photograph. His hair was still cut very short, and there was grey in it now, at the sides, though he was only thirty-nine. He was wearing a plain white T-shirt and work boots. He looked like what he was: a mechanic from New Mexico on his day off.
I had not seen him in the flesh since the day of his sentencing, in a courtroom in Albuquerque, in 2020, when I had sat at the back, in sunglasses, and left before he turned round.

He did not come towards me. He waited. I walked across the plaza to him, through the people, and stopped about six feet away, the way you stand from a patient’s family when you are about to tell them something.
“Hey,” he said.
“Hey.”
He looked at my face for a long time. Then he said, “You look like hell, Dana.”

And I laughed. I could not help it. It came up out of me like being sick, a horrible, cracked, helpless laugh, and he smiled, a little, at the corner of his mouth, the way he used to, and for one second we were two people at a Christmas party, and then we were not.

I said it then. On the plaza, at about a quarter past one on a Sunday afternoon, with the trolley bell ringing and a family next to us arguing about which way to the car park. In daylight, with people walking past. The way Chela had said I should.
I am going to put it down exactly, because I have tried, since, to remember every word, and I think this is right.

I said: “I was driving. I had been drinking. I took your keys out of your pocket and I drove your truck and I was looking at the radio and I killed him. And then I made you say it was you. I begged you. It was my idea. All of it. And he was alive, Wes. He was alive for eight minutes, and I knew what to do, and I didn’t go to him. I stood at the door and wiped the wheel. And then I let you go to prison for it. And I never came. Not once. Not one time. I’m sorry. I’m so sorry.”
That last part I had never said to anyone. Chela had been right. Six hours in the night, and I had not said it once.

It is not much of a sentence. I’m sorry. I have said it to families a thousand times at work. I’m so sorry for your loss. It is the most worn-out sentence in the English language. I said it anyway, because it was the only one I had, and because it was true, and because it was not too late, for him.
Wes listened to all of it without moving.
When I had finished he said: “I know.”
That was all. I know.
“I was there,” he said.
We sat on a low concrete wall at the edge of the plaza, in the shade of the palm trees, with a space between us the width of a person.
He told me some things. Not many. He was never a talker.

He told me that prison had been about what I would imagine, and that he did not want to talk about it, and that the worst part had not been prison. The worst part had been the first year, when he waited for me to come.

He told me that he had gone to the white house in 2024 because he could not sleep, because every night in his cell and every night after he had heard the sound from the ditch. That he had gone because a man he worked with, who used to be on heroin, had gone and come back clean, and told him about it. That he had not wanted to see anything. He had only wanted to sleep.

He told me that on his grey day, in the leather chair, Chela had told him who she was, and he had told her the thing about the ditch, and that she had held his hand, and they had both cried, and then she had gone home, and he had never seen her again either.
“She sends me photographs,” he said. “Of the sea. Once a month. No words. Just the sea.”
He told me that he had kept the cross.

“After she moved to Mexico,” he said. “Somebody had to. It was falling down. The bicycle was all faded.” He looked at his boots. “I moved back to Albuquerque last year. I go on Sundays. I fixed it up. Put a new bike on it. I go after church. I don’t even go to church. I just say that.”
I asked him why he had come today.
He thought about it for a long time, the way he used to think about an engine before he touched it.

“I wanted to see if you’d say it,” he said. “That’s all. I didn’t know if you would. I thought maybe you’d walk out of there and see me and turn round and go back into Mexico.” He almost smiled. “That’s what you would have done before.”
“Yes,” I said. “It is.”
I asked him what he wanted me to do.
“There’s nothing anybody can do,” I said. “Chela told me. The law’s run out. They can’t charge me now. It ran out last Christmas.”
“I know,” he said. “She told me too.”
“But your record,” I said. “It still says you. For the rest of your life, it says you killed a child with your truck. Every job you go for. Every apartment. Every time a cop runs your licence.”
“Yes.”

“I could make a statement,” I said. “To the police. In writing. Sworn. I could tell them. They can’t charge me, but they’d have it. On the file. It’s not much. It might not change anything. But it would be there.”
He looked at me.
“And your job?” he said.
I did not answer for a moment.

I knew what would happen. A respiratory therapist who drove drunk and killed a child and lied about it to the police and let another man go to prison for her and left a dying boy in a ditch, a boy she knew how to save, because she was frightened for her future. I knew exactly what would happen to my licence. I would never stand at the head of a bed again. I would never hold the bag again, and count, and keep someone breathing.
The only thing in my life I had ever been really good at.
“It would go,” I said.
He nodded slowly.

“I’m not going to tell you to do it,” he said. “I’m done telling you things, and I’m done doing things because you ask. That’s what got us here.” He stood up off the wall and put his hands back in his pockets. “You do what you do, Dana. I’ll be at the cross on Sunday. Same as always. Ten o’clock.”
He looked at me one more time.
“He wasn’t scared, you know,” he said. “At the end. I want you to know that. He wasn’t scared. He was just asking for his mom.”

Then he walked away across the plaza, through the people, towards a dusty blue pickup truck in the car park on the other side of the road, and got in on the driver’s side, and drove away north, and did not look back.
It is twelve hours from San Diego to Albuquerque.

I drove it through the night, the way I had come, in reverse: up into the mountains and down into the desert, across the river at Yuma, through the heat of Phoenix, up onto the high country at Flagstaff, east along the interstate in the dark, past Gallup and the red rocks.

I passed the eleven descansos again. I counted them again. This time I looked at every one. I slowed down and looked at each of them straight on, in my headlights, the white crosses and the plastic flowers and the names, all eleven, one after another, in the dark.
I did not have the radio on. I did not take my pill. I had thrown the bottle into a bin in the car park at San Ysidro, before I got in the car.
I got to Albuquerque at about half past three in the morning on Monday. I did not go home.
I drove to the North Valley, and I took the road. The one I had driven a long way round for nearly seven years.
The cross was where it had always been, at the edge of the ditch.

Wes had kept it well. The wood was freshly painted white, very bright in my headlights. The little plastic bicycle tied to it was new, a bright blue one, with green garden wire twisted round the crossbar to hold it. There were plastic flowers in a jar, red and white, for Christmas already. And there was a small photograph in a frame, behind plastic, of a boy of twelve with a gap in his front teeth, grinning, in a dark blue jacket.
MATEO ORTIZ, it said, in black letters on the crossbar. And two dates, twelve years apart.
I turned the engine off. I turned the lights off. I got out of the car into the cold.

It was very dark, the way it had been that night. The same trees. The same black ditch, with the water low in it. The same stars. Somewhere a dog barked, at the Archuleta place, I suppose, though it could not be the same dog.
I knelt down in the dirt in front of the cross.
I did not pray. I do not know how. I did not say anything to him. I had nothing to say to him that would mean anything. He was twelve. He was asking for his mother.
What I did was count.
I counted the way we are taught. Once every six seconds. Ten to a minute. And at the end of every minute, its number, out loud, softly, in the dark, on my knees beside the ditch.
One. Two. Three.
It was the counting from the dream. It was the counting from the road. It was the counting I had done at the door of the truck, wiping the wheel, without even knowing I was doing it.
Four. Five.

Only this time I knew what I was counting. I was counting the minutes that boy had been alive in the ditch while I stood twenty feet away. I was counting what I had owed him. I was going to count all of them, out loud, one after another, so that somebody, finally, had sat at the side of this road and counted them on purpose.
Six. Seven.
At eight I stopped.

I knelt there in the cold with my mouth open and the number nine in it, and I could not say it. Not because the medicine would not let me. Because nine was not mine. Nine was the minute after. Nine was the minute Wes took his phone out and called. Nine was the call. After nine, they came and asked who was driving, and I said—
I took my phone out of my coat.
My hands were very cold, and very steady. I have never shaken, at work, in six years. I did not shake now.

I did not call the newspaper, or a lawyer, or my mother, or my manager at the hospital. I called the number for the sheriff’s office, the ordinary one, not the emergency one, that I found on the website in the dark with my thumb.
It rang a long time. It was four in the morning on a Monday.
A woman answered. She sounded tired. She sounded like someone on a night shift.
I said, “I’d like to make a statement about a fatal accident. Twenty-first of December, 2019. North Valley. A boy on a bicycle.”
She said, “Is this an emergency, ma’am?”
I looked at the cross, at the boy in the frame with the gap in his teeth.
“No,” I said. “It was. Not any more.”
She said, “Okay. Can I take your name?”
And I gave it to her.

I said it slowly, the way you say a name to somebody who is writing it down. Then I spelled it for her, letter by letter, so that she would get it right. So that it would be on the file, in the right place, at last, in the driver’s seat, where it belonged.
WHAT IT DID

Ibogaine, from the root bark of Tabernanthe iboga [tah-ber-NAN-thee ih-BOH-gah], a shrub of the rainforest of west-central Africa. Grown. The root has been eaten in Gabon for longer than anyone has written down; the molecule was first drawn out of it in 1901. Door: leaving the body.

How it was taken in this book. Once, by mouth, as capsules of a purified extract, in a private clinic in Mexico, lying on a bed, with a heart monitor attached, a drip of magnesium and potassium, a doctor in the house and a sitter beside her all night. A single test capsule in the late afternoon; then the full dose in two parts, an hour apart, at nine and ten at night.

How long. It began within the hour, with a buzzing. The visions ran from about ten at night until nearly six in the morning. Then the grey day: a day and a night more, awake, unable to sleep, the body heavy and the mind turning. The liver makes a second substance from the first, noribogaine [nor-ih-BOH-gah-een], and it stays in the blood for a day or two more. Altogether, about thirty hours before she slept, and days before she felt like herself.

What it did to time. Inside the night, time ran like a film: years in seconds, and then one night on a county road, which went on for most of the night. Outside, a sitter wrote the clock time beside everything she said.

What it did to the body. Nausea and vomiting. She could not walk or stand without falling. Her heart slowed, and the interval in each beat that lets the heart reset itself grew long. At 02:40 her heart fell into a dangerous rhythm, torsades de pointes [tor-SAHD duh PWANT], and the monitor’s alarm went off. Ten minutes later the doctor pushed magnesium into her vein, and within a minute or so the rhythm came back. She had hidden a medicine that made this more likely.
What it did to the self. She was not one person. She was in two places at once: on a bed in Mexico, and on the road in December
2019. And on the road she was not herself. She was the boy, then the man beside her, then herself at the driver’s door, then the boy’s mother, and last of all, herself in the ditch.

What it did to the world. First a buzzing, and a ticking like a bicycle wheel. Trails behind moving hands. Then a film of her life, very fast, and then the one night, very slow, seen from every seat in the truck, and from the ditch, and from a hospital laundry across town.
What it meant. She came out of it knowing she could no longer say the sentence she had said for nearly seven years. It did not take anything off her. It put everything on.
What it did not do. It did not let her sleep that night, or the day after. It did not forgive her. It did not tell anyone else what she had seen. She had to do that herself.
On the strength scale made by the chemist Alexander Shulgin: plus three, the full effect, impossible to ignore.
THE MAPMAKER
For Howard Lotsof (1943–2010) and for James W. Fernandez, who listened to the Bwiti
Howard Stephen Lotsof was born on 1 March 1943, in the Bronx, the only child of Abner and Lillian Lotsof.

In 1962 he was nineteen, and addicted to heroin, and looking for a new high. Somebody had a bitter white powder, a chemical drawn from the root of a shrub that grows in Gabon, in Africa. Almost nothing was known about it outside Africa. He took it to see what it would do.

What it did, he said, was give him a long and strange night of visions, and a morning on which he no longer wanted heroin. There was no sickness of withdrawal. The want was simply gone. He gave the powder to six friends who were also addicted. Five of them, he said, stopped.

He spent the rest of his life trying to make the world take that seriously. He was not a doctor or a scientist. He left one university, and years later graduated from New York University, in 1976. He had studied film.

In 1985 he was granted the first of a series of United States patents for using ibogaine to interrupt addiction to narcotics. The last of them was granted in 1992. In the 1980s he persuaded a company in Belgium to make capsules of it for addicts in the Netherlands, and worked with a Dutch psychiatrist, Jan Bastiaans [yahn BAHS-tee-ahns], treating people there. He wrote and co-wrote papers in medical journals. He founded the Dora Weiner Foundation, named for his grandmother, to help people find treatment and to push for research.

He knocked on doors at the drug companies and in government, and in the end, one opened. The National Institute on Drug Abuse studied ibogaine in the 1990s, and the work it paid for filled the journals and led the Food and Drug Administration to approve a trial in people. The trial was never finished. There were disputes over contracts, and the money ran out. Ibogaine remains illegal in the United States, in the same class as heroin.
He was never short of critics, and some of them were serious people. They pointed out that there were no controlled studies, and that people had died. They were right about both.
Howard Lotsof died on 31 January 2010, at a hospital near his home on Staten Island, of cancer of the liver. He was sixty-six. His wife, Norma, whom he married in 1964, survived him.

Almost every clinic that offers ibogaine today, on either side of any border, exists because of one night when he was nineteen. This book is dedicated to him because he was the first outsider to come back from that night and say, out loud and for the rest of his life, what it had done.
James W. Fernandez

Long before the clinics, the root belonged to the people of the forest, and it still does. The Fang [FAHNG] people of Gabon and their neighbours built a religion around it, Bwiti, which mixes their own old faith in the ancestors with things they took from Christianity, and keeps them both.

Most of what outsiders know about Bwiti comes from one patient man. James W. Fernandez, an American anthropologist born in Chicago in 1930, first worked in Gabon in the late 1950s, and went back in 1960 to live among the Fang, at their chapels and their all-night ceremonies. He did not go to take anything from them. He went to listen. His book, Bwiti: An Ethnography of the Religious Imagination in Africa, published by Princeton University Press in 1982, is still the place almost everyone begins.

He went on to teach at Dartmouth, Princeton and the University of Chicago, where he is professor emeritus. As this book went to press he was living, and this page says only what is in his public record.
The book does not end with him. Bwiti is not a museum. It belongs to the people who keep it, and much of what they know is theirs and is not written here.
The people around them
Jean Dybowski and Édouard Landrin [zhahn dih-BOF-skee, ay-DWAR lahn-DRAN], who in 1901 first drew the active substance out of the root, in France, and named it.

The makers of Lambarène [lahm-bah-REN], a French medicine sold from the 1930s until 1966 as a mild tonic against tiredness, made from a related plant. It was named after Lambaréné [lahm-bah-ray-NAY], a town on the Ogooué [oh-goh-WAY] River in Gabon.
Kenneth Alper and his colleagues, who in 2012 went through every death after ibogaine they could find outside Africa, and counted them.

Eduardo Schenberg and his colleagues in Brazil, who in 2017 asked patients what the night was like and wrote down what they said: difficult, physical, full of memories, and like a rehearsal of danger.
Marcus Capone, who took it in Mexico in 2017, and with his wife, Amber, has helped hundreds of other veterans to do the same.
Nolan Williams and his colleagues at Stanford University, who in 2024 published a study of thirty special-forces veterans treated with ibogaine and magnesium at a clinic in Mexico.
Kevin Franciotti, who went to a clinic in Baja California and wrote down the grey day honestly.
